title: He did not lose wisdom first.
paragraphs:
He did not lose wisdom first.
He lost wonder.
And that is how even the wisest man who ever lived began to fall.
Let that settle in your chest for a moment.

Because the story of Solomon in 1 Kings 11 is not just ancient history.
It is a mirror.

A mirror for every gifted leader.
Every passionate believer.
Every person who once burned hot for God.
Solomon started well.

God gave him wisdom no king had ever possessed.
Kings traveled across deserts just to hear him speak.
Gold flooded his kingdom.
Peace filled his borders.
And he built the temple of the Lord.
Imagine that.
A man entrusted with constructing the dwelling place of God on earth.

Yet the same man who built the house of God…
eventually built altars for other gods.
That is the quiet horror of 1 Kings 11.
Scripture says:

“For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God.”
— 1 Kings 11:4
Not wholly true.
Those three words carry the weight of a broken kingdom.
Solomon did not wake up one morning and decide to rebel against God.
No.
His heart drifted slowly.

One compromise.
One forbidden alliance.
One affection that God had already warned him about.
Then another.
And another.
Until a thousand relationships surrounded the throne of Israel — wives and concubines from nations God had specifically warned him not to marry.
But understand something deeper here.
The danger was not merely romance.
It was influence.
Because the people closest to your heart will always shape the direction of your worship.
And Solomon — the man who wrote Proverbs about guarding the heart — allowed his own heart to be divided.
That is the terrifying irony.

You can speak wisdom…
and still ignore it.

You can teach truth…
and slowly drift away from it.

You can build monuments to God publicly…
while secretly building altars to idols in your private life.
The Bible says Solomon followed Ashtoreth, Milcom, and other gods.
He built high places.
He tolerated worship that dishonored the God who had given him everything.
And God was angry.
Not because God is insecure.
But because God is holy.
And because idolatry always destroys the one who practices it.
The king who once asked God for wisdom ended his story with a divided heart.
And if we are honest, that reality should shake every one of us.
Because the seeds of Solomon’s fall still exist today.
Idolatry rarely looks like statues and incense in modern life.
It looks like success that becomes identity.
It looks like relationships that slowly pull us away from obedience.
It looks like ambition that replaces devotion.
It looks like secret habits that quietly compete for the throne of our hearts.
And the scariest part?
You can still look spiritual while your heart is drifting.
Solomon still ruled.
Still wrote.
Still appeared powerful.
But his heart was no longer fully the Lord’s.
And that is the danger of a divided heart.
But this story is not only about Solomon’s failure.
It is about our need for a better king.
Solomon was wise.
But Jesus is perfect wisdom.
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus became the temple.
Solomon allowed his heart to be divided.
Jesus loved the Father with perfect obedience.
Where Solomon compromised…
Jesus conquered.
Where Solomon’s choices fractured the kingdom…
Jesus’ sacrifice restores sinners.
And this is the Gospel.
Jesus does not come for people who have never drifted.
He comes for people whose hearts have wandered.
People who built altars they never meant to build.
People who once loved God fiercely but slowly lost their wonder.
If that is you today…
Hear this clearly.
Grace is still calling your name.
The cross of Christ is proof that your story does not have to end where Solomon’s drift began.
Jesus died for idol-makers.
Jesus restores wandering hearts.
Jesus rebuilds what sin tries to destroy.
So the real question is not whether idols exist in our world.
The question is this:
What is sitting on the throne of your heart right now?
Success?
Approval?
Pleasure?
Control?
Or Jesus?
Because the human heart was never designed to worship many things.
It was created to worship One.
And when Christ becomes the center again…
Everything else falls back into its rightful place.
So today, examine your heart.
Not with shame.
But with honesty.
Tear down every altar that competes with Christ.
Return to the King who never drifts.
Return to the Savior who never divides His love.
Return to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy in Scripture is not Solomon’s fall.
The greatest tragedy would be ignoring the warning it gives us.
Guard your heart.
Protect your worship.
And never forget who truly deserves the throne.
Jesus Christ.
The better King.
Someone who might be drifting quietly.
Someone who needs to know it is not too late to return.
Because the Gospel still rescues wandering hearts.
